blocks.prompt: 1 (i) Find the inverses of the following matrices by using row operations: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
The matrix must first be non-singular; row operations will show it.
We must find \(A^{-1}\) or show that it does not exist.
Plan: reduce \([A \mid I_3]\); watch for a zero row on the left, then confirm with \(|A|\).
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6\end{bmatrix}\)
To find: \(A^{-1}\) by row operations.
Method: Write \(A\) and \(I_3\) side by side as \([A \mid I_3]\). Use row operations to turn the left half into \(I_3\); the right half then becomes \(A^{-1}\). If the left half gets a whole row of zeros, \(A\) is singular and has no inverse.

Append \(I_3\) on the right
\[\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\]
Why: Every row operation is done on the whole row, both halves together. Column 1 already has a leading 1 in \(R_1\) and a 0 in \(R_2\).

Read the result: a zero row on the left
Row 3 of the left half is \((0, 0, 0)\). No row operation can now make a leading 1 in that row, so the left half can never become \(I_3\).
Why: Row operations never change whether a determinant is zero, so a zero row means \(|A| = 0\).

Check with the determinant
\[|A| = \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 6\end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 1(-12 - 0) - 2(0 - 0) - 3(0 - 4)\]
\[= -12 + 0 + 12\]
\[= 0\]
Why: Expanding along \(R_1\) confirms \(|A| = 0\): \(A\) is singular.
blocks.final_answer: \(|A| = 0\): the matrix as printed is singular, so \(A^{-1}\) does not exist.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & \frac{17}{4} & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{11}{6} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\) as the inverse for 1(i). The printed matrix has \(|A| = 0\), so it has no inverse at all. The key's matrix is in fact the inverse of \(\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 5 & 6\end{bmatrix}\), a different matrix (perhaps the one intended; its determinant is \(-12\)). For the question as printed the correct answer is: the inverse does not exist.

blocks.prompt: 1 (ii) Find the inverses of the following matrices by using row operations: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
A \(3 \times 3\) inverse by row operations (Gauss-Jordan).
We must find \(A^{-1}\).
Plan: check \(|A| \neq 0\), reduce \([A \mid I_3]\) column by column (pivot 1, zeros above and below), read the right half, check \(AA^{-1} = I_3\).
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\)
To find: \(A^{-1}\) by row operations.
Method: First check \(|A| \neq 0\). Then reduce \([A \mid I_3]\) until the left half is \(I_3\); the right half is then \(A^{-1}\).

Append \(I_3\) on the right
\[\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\]
Why: Whatever we do to the rows of \(A\), we also do to \(I_3\).

Make the pivot of \(R_2\) equal to 1
By \(\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)R_2 \to R_2'\)
\(R_2'\): \(0\), \(1\), \(-4\) | \(0\), \(-\frac{1}{2}\), \(0\)
\[\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & -1 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\]
Why: Dividing \(R_2\) by \(-2\) turns \(-2\) into the leading 1 of row 2.

Make the pivot of \(R_3\) equal to 1
By \(\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)R_3 \to R_3'\)
\(R_3'\): \(0\), \(0\), \(1\) | \(\frac{1}{5}\), \(\frac{1}{5}\), \(-\frac{1}{5}\)
\[\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 0 & 7 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{5} & \frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5}\end{array}\right]\]
Why: Dividing \(R_3\) by \(-5\) gives the third leading 1.

Read off the inverse
\[A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & \frac{7}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{10} & -\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{1}{5} & \frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: The left half is \(I_3\), so the right half is \(A^{-1}\).

Check: \(AA^{-1} = I_3\)
Row 1 of \(A\) times each column of \(A^{-1}\): \((1)\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right) + (2)\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) + (-1)\left(\frac{1}{5}\right) = 1\), \((1)\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right) + (2)\left(\frac{3}{10}\right) + (-1)\left(\frac{1}{5}\right) = 0\), \((1)\left(\frac{7}{5}\right) + (2)\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right) + (-1)\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right) = 0\). Rows 2 and 3 give \((0, 1, 0)\) and \((0, 0, 1)\) in the same way.
\[AA^{-1} = I_3 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A matrix times its inverse must give the identity matrix.

blocks.prompt: 1 (iii) Find the inverses of the following matrices by using row operations: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 13 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
A \(3 \times 3\) inverse by row operations (Gauss-Jordan).
We must find \(A^{-1}\).
Plan: check \(|A| \neq 0\), reduce \([A \mid I_3]\) column by column (pivot 1, zeros above and below), read the right half, check \(AA^{-1} = I_3\).
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 13 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\)
To find: \(A^{-1}\) by row operations.
Method: First check \(|A| \neq 0\). Then reduce \([A \mid I_3]\) until the left half is \(I_3\); the right half is then \(A^{-1}\).

Append \(I_3\) on the right
\[\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 6 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 13 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\]
Why: Whatever we do to the rows of \(A\), we also do to \(I_3\).

Make the pivot of \(R_3\) equal to 1
By \(\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)R_3 \to R_3'\)
\(R_3'\): \(0\), \(0\), \(1\) | \(\frac{2}{3}\), \(-\frac{1}{3}\), \(-\frac{1}{3}\)
\[\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 0 & 26 & 13 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3}\end{array}\right]\]
Why: Dividing \(R_3\) by \(-3\) gives the third leading 1.

Read off the inverse
\[A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{13}{3} & \frac{8}{3} & \frac{26}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: The left half is \(I_3\), so the right half is \(A^{-1}\).

Check: \(AA^{-1} = I_3\)
Row 1 of \(A\) times each column of \(A^{-1}\): \((1)\left(-\frac{13}{3}\right) + (6)\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) + (2)\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = 1\), \((1)\left(\frac{8}{3}\right) + (6)\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) + (2)\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = 0\), \((1)\left(\frac{26}{3}\right) + (6)\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) + (2)\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = 0\). Rows 2 and 3 give \((0, 1, 0)\) and \((0, 0, 1)\) in the same way.
\[AA^{-1} = I_3 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A matrix times its inverse must give the identity matrix.
